summary: Gives authors of Reliable Multicast Transport building block and protocol definitions guidelines so their documents fully explain operation and use. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a checklist for writers of technical documents so their instructions are complete.

questions: how to write rmt protocol specifications
subtitle: A checklist for documenting reliable multicast building blocks and protocols.

tldr.problem: Reliable Multicast Transport (RMT) protocols are complex, and authors need clear guidance on how to document building blocks and protocol instantiations so others can understand, reuse, and combine them safely.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC provides detailed checklists and section requirements for building block documents (rationale, functionality, applicability, security) and protocol instantiation documents (applicability, architecture, conformance, functionality, packet formats).
tldr.outcome: Well-structured RMT documentation enables modular, reusable components that can be combined into new reliable multicast protocols for diverse scenarios and requirements.

today: RFC 3269 is an Informational RFC providing best-practice guidelines for the RMT working group. It remains the authoritative source for how to document reliable multicast building blocks and protocol instantiations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Reliable Multicast Transport (RMT) protocols deliver messages to many receivers over a network while ensuring every receiver gets every message in order. Different applications need different trade-offs: some value speed, others reliability, and some prioritize handling many simultaneous receivers.

Rather than building each protocol from scratch, the RMT approach uses building blocks, reusable components that provide specific functionality (such as loss detection or congestion control) that can be combined into different protocol instantiations for different scenarios. The same building block can appear in multiple protocols, and can be improved over time as experience grows.

However, this modular approach creates a risk: building blocks have dependencies and limitations. Block A might work with B, B with C, but A with C might fail. This document provides guidelines to ensure that building block and protocol specifications clearly document these constraints and dependencies.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of building each multicast protocol from the ground up, builders use reusable pieces called building blocks. This RFC explains how authors should document these pieces so they can be safely combined into working protocols.

sections.title: Building Block Document Requirements
sections.content:
A building block document must define one self-contained piece of functionality that can be reused across multiple protocols. It MUST include the following sections:

Rationale explains why this particular function needs its own building block. It must justify the granularity: if the block is too small, implementations will be trivial and burdensome; if too large, the block becomes specific to a single protocol and loses reusability.

Functionality describes all algorithms and functions in the block and specifies the external interfaces that allow other building blocks to connect to it. External interfaces are critical for combining blocks into working protocols.

Applicability Statement is one of the most important sections. It identifies when the building block can and cannot be used: intended scenarios, known failure modes, environmental considerations (single-source multicast, satellite networks, wireless networks, asymmetric networks), and conflicts or incompatibilities with other blocks.

Packet-Header Fields specify what protocol message information the block needs. Most blocks describe generic header fields; others specify abstract messages. Security considerations must be addressed when a block raises special security issues.

Requirements from other Building Blocks exhaustively lists what the block needs from other blocks to work correctly: event generation, message ordering, and other dependencies.
sections.plainLanguage: When authors describe a building block, they must explain what it does, how it connects to other blocks, when to use it, what it needs from other blocks, and any security issues it raises. This helps builders understand how to use it safely.

sections.title: Protocol Instantiation Document Requirements
sections.content:
A protocol instantiation document shows how to combine multiple building blocks into a complete, working protocol. It MUST include four sections:

Applicability Statement frames the design space. It identifies the target application (real-time delivery or file transfer), the target scale (maximum number of receivers), the intended environments (asymmetric, wireless, satellite networks), and any environments where the protocol should not be used. It also documents known weaknesses and spectacular failure modes that can occur under certain conditions.

Architecture Definition provides an overview of how the protocol operates, which building blocks it uses with references to their documents, how the blocks are joined together, and the design trade-offs made in selecting the architecture.

Conformance Statement includes a mandatory paragraph asserting that the document, together with the building block documents it references, completely specifies a working reliable multicast transport protocol that meets the requirements of RFC 2357. This ensures the protocol protects the network from failures as well as unicast transport protocols do.

Functionality Definition provides complete algorithmic specifications for each building block, additional functionality specific to this protocol, a description of how each building block is used in accordance with its applicability statement, and an abstract programming interface for application integration.

Packet Formats specify the exact message format for both IPv4 and IPv6, show IPSEC support explicitly, and document how message parts are concatenated. Protocols initially use UDP; a dedicated IP protocol number is considered only after widespread deployment and understanding.
sections.plainLanguage: When authors combine building blocks into a complete protocol, they must explain what problems it solves, what blocks it uses, how they fit together, what it works for (and what it does not), exactly how messages are formatted, and how applications will use it.

sections.title: Security and Codepoint Considerations
sections.content:
Security considerations fall to the protocol instantiation document rather than individual building blocks, and must comply with RFC 2357. However, a building block specification MUST address special security issues if the block involves exchange of sensitive data or if its nature creates security risks.

Some building blocks (such as Forward Error Correction) describe general frameworks that leave specific algorithms to implementation. When a building block leaves implementation details open, authors MUST address codepoint considerations: how will specific algorithms, options, or code points be registered with IANA and made extensible for future implementations?
sections.plainLanguage: Security issues belong in the final protocol, not in individual building blocks, unless a block handles sensitive data. Some blocks define frameworks with room for different algorithms; those blocks need to explain how to add new algorithms over time.

sections.title: Documentation Checklists
sections.content:
RFC 3269 provides summary checklists for authors to verify completeness. Building block documents require sections covering rationale (with justification and granularity rationale), functionality (functions and interfaces), applicability statement (intended use, failure modes, environmental considerations, incompatibilities), packet header fields (where applicable), requirements from other blocks, and security considerations (where applicable).

Protocol instantiation documents require applicability statement (application space, scale, environments, weaknesses), architecture definition (operational overview, building blocks used, joining details, trade-offs), conformance statement (the mandatory paragraph), functionality definition (algorithmic specs, additional functionality, compliance with building block applicability), and packet formats (IPv4, IPv6, IPSEC, message ordering).

These checklists ensure that authors address all critical elements needed for others to understand, implement, and reuse their specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC includes two checklists: one for building block authors to verify they have explained what the block does and when to use it, and one for protocol authors to ensure their complete protocol specification covers all important details.
